title: Predicting Final Mathematics Grades Based on Student Demographics
text:
The question
In one or two short paragraphs, introduce the setting, audience, focused research question, data source, observational unit, response, important predictors, and one important data limitation. Lead with what makes the question worth answering.
Our question that we’re looking at with this data is how well can we predict a student’s final grade in mathematics based on their demographics and characteristics? Because our data is specifically from Portuguese schools, the question is first applicable to Portuguese schools, even if it can eventually be generalized to schools in different languages as well. This research question can help inform school counselors, school districts, and even the student’s families to help them identify some students who may be at risk of failing or getting lower grades, and thus help those students by providing support in whichever way possible. By doing this analysis, it could help understand what effects a students grade and see if we can predict what their final grade is so that support can be offered to help them improve it.
Our response variable is the final grade (G3). There are 32 predictors total and some of the predictors we believe will be important are the number of past class failures, the student’s sex and age, whether they live somewhere urban or rural, who their guardian is (mother, father, or other), their level of weekend alcohol consumption, and whether they take extra paid classes within their math class. The observational unit from the data is a secondary education student in mathematics at one of two Portuguese schools. One limitation for this data set is the fact that it’s based on different questionaires that the students took, meaning it can be more subjective.
This is our citation for the data we will be using throughout this project: Cortez, P. (2008). Student Performance [Dataset]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. https://doi.org/10.24432/C5TG7T.

title: Predicting Final Mathematics Grades Based on Student Demographics
text:
What the baseline shows
Describe and justify a simple course-based baseline regression model. Interpret the result that best establishes the rest of the story, including its direction, magnitude, scale, and uncertainty. Explain one limitation or unresolved pattern that motivates deeper analysis.
We did this baseline model because it included a lot of the different predictors that we were interested in seeing their relationship with a student’s final grade, and a lot of them we saw at least a minor difference in the initial plots.
Interpreting the coefficient for the failures predictor:
Assuming that the assumptions behind this model are accurate and multicollinearity is not a big issue, then holding a student’s gender, age, geographical address(urban vs. rural), guardian, weekly alcohol content, and whether or not they’re paying for outside support (like tutors) constant, an increase of one past failed class is typically associated with an estimated 1.8989 decrease in average final grade in mathematics for a student at one of these two Portuguese schools. And, again only if the assumptions hold, we are 95% confident that the true coefficient for the association between past class failures and a student’s final grade in math is between a 2.547 decrease in final grade to a 1.251 decrease on average.
There’s a lot of room for improvement from this initial model. We haven’t done any diagnostic tests to see if this model is appropriate for our data and if the inferences we make are justified. We also don’t know if there is a relationship between any of the predictors that we used so we might also have a multicollinearity issue which would make the coefficient estimates unstable. On top of all of that, these might not be the best predictors at explaining the data, or predicting a student’s final grade, especially since we just picked them by looking at the initial one-at-a-time plots. There’s probably a better combination of predictors that would be better at predicting a response and we’ll have to do more analysis to figure out which ones those are.
